decision.explanation: The characteristic roots are ±2i, giving fundamental solutions cos(2x) and sin(2x). Their derivatives give A=[[0,2],[0,2]], so det(A)=0. Uniqueness requires det(A)≠0. Here every y(x)=C cos(2x) satisfies both boundary conditions, so there are infinitely many solutions.

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ 

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=0,{\beta }_{i}=1,a=0,$ and $b=\pi ,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(\pi ) & {y}_{2}^{′}(\pi )\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 2\text{i}.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\text{ and }{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x,\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \pi ) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =0\cdot 2-2\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)=0$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has infinitely many solutions}.$

y″+4y=0,y′(0)=y′(π)=0,0≤x≤π

Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ 

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Neumann boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=0,{\beta }_{i}=1,a=0,$ and $b=\pi ,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(0) & {y}_{2}^{′}(0) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(\pi ) & {y}_{2}^{′}(\pi )\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+4 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 2\text{i}.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x\text{ and }{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x,\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot 0) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \pi ) & 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \pi )\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =0\cdot 2-2\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)=0$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has infinitely many solutions}.$

after.worked_solution:
To solve the homogeneous boundary value problem, we first find the general solution and then determine the values of the arbitrary constants that fit the boundary conditions.

We have the equation

$$
{y}^{″}(x)=0.
$$

Integrating this equation twice, we get the general solution

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}^{′}=A.
$$

Applying the condition $y(3)=0,$ we have

$$
3A+B=0\,⇒\,B=-3A.
$$

So, we have

$$
y=Ax-3A=A(x-3).
$$

Applying the condition $y(5)-2{y}^{′}(5)=0,$ we have

$$
2A-2A=0
$$

which is automatically satisfied for any $A.$

Therefore, the solution to the BVP is $y=A\cdot (x-3),$ where $A$ is arbitrary.

decision.explanation: Uniqueness holds exactly when det(A)≠0. The characteristic equation (m-1)(m-3)=0 gives fundamental solutions e^x and e^(3x). Thus A=[[e,e^3],[e^3,3e^9]], and det(A)=3e^10-e^6=e^6(3e^4-1)≠0. Therefore the unique solution is y≡0.

after.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}(x)+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0,
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$   

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$
In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Robin boundary conditions given by

$$
y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(3)=0.
$$

So, setting ${\alpha }_{1}=1,$ ${\beta }_{1}=0,$ ${\alpha }_{2}=0,$ ${\beta }_{2}=1,$ and $a=1,$ $b=3,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(3) & {y}_{2}^{′}(3)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-4m+3 & =0 \\ (m-1)(m-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have ${m}_{1}=1$ and ${m}_{2}=3,$ and so the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}\,\text{and}\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=3{e}^{3x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{1} & {e}^{3(1)} \\ {e}^{3} & 3{e}^{3(3)}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}e & {e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & 3{e}^{9}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =e(3{e}^{9})-{e}^{3}({e}^{3}) \\  & =3{e}^{10}-{e}^{6} \\  & ={e}^{6}(3{e}^{4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

y″(x)+P(x)y′(x)+Q(x)y=0,a≤x≤b

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

α1y(a)+β1y′(a)=0,α2y(b)+β2y′(b)=0, where P and Q are continuous on [a,b], and αi,βi are real constants such that (αi,βi)≠(0,0). Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are y1(x) and y2(x).

Now, let's define the following matrix:

A=[α1y1(a)+β1y1′(a)α1y2(a)+β1y2′(a)α2y1(b)+β2y1′(b)α2y2(b)+β2y2′(b)].

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution y≡0 if and only if det(A)≠0.
In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

Notice that, in our case, we have Robin boundary conditions given by
y(1)=0,y′(3)=0. So, setting α1=1, β1=0, α2=0, β2=1, and a=1, b=3, the matrix A reduces to

A=[y1(1)y2(1)y1′(3)y2′(3)].

To find the fundamental solutions, we set y=emx. The auxiliary equation is m2−4m+3=0(m−1)(m−3)=0. So, we have m1=1 and m2=3, and so the fundamental solutions are
y1(x)=exandy2(x)=e3x.

Differentiating, we have y1′(x)=ex,y2′(x)=3e3x.

Therefore, the matrix A is

A=[e1e3(1)e33e3(3)]=[ee3e33e9],

and we have det(A)=e(3e9)−e3(e3)=3e10−e6=e6(3e4−1).

Since det(A)≠0, we conclude that this BVP has the unique solution y≡0.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms all four answers: uniqueness requires det(A)≠0; the characteristic roots 1 and 3 give e^x and e^(3x); det(A)=e(3e^9)-e^3e^3=e^6(3e^4-1)≠0; hence y≡0 is the unique solution. The deliberately incorrect submission changed only the uniqueness criterion to det(A)=0.

Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}(x)+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0,
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$   

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}].
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$
In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Robin boundary conditions given by

$$
y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(3)=0.
$$

So, setting ${\alpha }_{1}=1,$ ${\beta }_{1}=0,$ ${\alpha }_{2}=0,$ ${\beta }_{2}=1,$ and $a=1,$ $b=3,$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(1) & {y}_{2}(1) \\ {y}_{1}^{′}(3) & {y}_{2}^{′}(3)\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-4m+3 & =0 \\ (m-1)(m-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have ${m}_{1}=1$ and ${m}_{2}=3,$ and so the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}\,\text{and}\,{y}_{2}(x)={e}^{3x}.
$$

Differentiating, we have

$$
{y}_{1}^{′}(x)={e}^{x},\,{y}_{2}^{′}(x)=3{e}^{3x}.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{1} & {e}^{3(1)} \\ {e}^{3} & 3{e}^{3(3)}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}e & {e}^{3} \\ {e}^{3} & 3{e}^{9}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =e(3{e}^{9})-{e}^{3}({e}^{3}) \\  & =3{e}^{10}-{e}^{6} \\  & ={e}^{6}(3{e}^{4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)\ne 0,$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has the unique solution }y≡0.$

A=[y1(1)y2(1)y1′(3)y2′(3)].

y1(x)=exandy2(x)=e3x.

Differentiating, we have y1′(x)=ex,y2′(x)=3e3x.

A=[e1e3(1)e33e3(3)]=[ee3e33e9],

and we have det(A)=e(3e9)−e3(e3)=3e10−e6=e6(3e4−1).

Since det(A)≠0, we conclude that this BVP has the unique solution y≡0.

decision.explanation: Uniqueness requires det(A)≠0. The characteristic roots ±2i give fundamental solutions sin(2x) and cos(2x). At both endpoints these have values 0 and -1, so A=[[0,-1],[0,-1]] and det(A)=0. Every y=C sin(2x) satisfies both boundary conditions, giving infinitely many solutions.

after.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ 

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=1,{\beta }_{i}=0,a=\frac{\pi }{2},$ and $b=\frac{3\pi }{2},$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & {y}_{2}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ {y}_{1}\,(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & {y}_{2}\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we solve the auxiliary equation

$$
{m}^{2}+4=0,
$$

which has roots $\pm 2i.$ Thus, the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\text{ and }{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi ) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(0)(-1)-(-1)(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)=0$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has infinitely many solutions.}$

EXPLANATION

Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

y″(x)+P(x)y′+Q(x)y=0,a≤x≤b

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

α1y(a)+β1y′(a)=0,α2y(b)+β2y′(b)=0 where P and Q are continuous on [a,b], and αi and βi are real constants such that (αi,βi)≠(0,0). Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are y1(x) and y2(x).

Now, let's define the following matrix:

A=[α1y1(a)+β1y1′(a)α1y2(a)+β1y2′(a)α2y1(b)+β2y1′(b)α2y2(b)+β2y2′(b)]

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution y≡0 if and only if det(A)≠0.

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has infinitely many solutions.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting αi=1,βi=0,a=π2, and b=3π2, the matrix A reduces to

A=[y1(π2)y2(π2)y1(3π2)y2(3π2)].

To find the fundamental solutions, we solve the auxiliary equation m2+4=0, which has roots ±2i. Thus, the fundamental solutions are y1(x)=sin⁡2x and y2(x)=cos⁡2x.

Therefore, the matrix A is A=[sin⁡(π)cos⁡(π)sin⁡(3π)cos⁡(3π)]=[0−10−1] and we have det(A)=(0)(−1)−(−1)(0)=0.

Since det(A)=0 we conclude that this BVP has infinitely many solutions.

content.worked_solution:
Suppose we have the second-order homogeneous boundary value (BVP) problem

$$
{y}^{″}(x)+P(x){y}^{′}+Q(x)y=0,\,a\le x\le b
$$

with the Robin (mixed) boundary conditions

$$
{\alpha }_{1}y(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}^{′}(a)=0,\,{\alpha }_{2}y(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}^{′}(b)=0
$$

where $P$ and $Q$ are continuous on $[a,b],$ and ${\alpha }_{i}$ and ${\beta }_{i}$ are real constants such that $({\alpha }_{i},{\beta }_{i})\ne (0,0).$ Furthermore, suppose the fundamental solutions to the equation are ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x).$ 

Now, let's define the following matrix:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\,{\alpha }_{1}{y}_{1}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}(a) & {\alpha }_{1}{y}_{2}(a)+{\beta }_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}(a) \\ {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{1}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}(b) & {\alpha }_{2}{y}_{2}(b)+{\beta }_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}(b)\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the BVP has a unique, trivial solution $y≡0$ if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

In other words, if the determinant equals zero, then the BVP has *infinitely many solutions*.

Notice that, in our case, we have Dirichlet boundary conditions. So, setting ${\alpha }_{i}=1,{\beta }_{i}=0,a=\frac{\pi }{2},$ and $b=\frac{3\pi }{2},$ the matrix $A$ reduces to

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) & {y}_{2}\,(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ {y}_{1}\,(\frac{3\pi }{2}) & {y}_{2}\,(\frac{3\pi }{2})\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the fundamental solutions, we solve the auxiliary equation

$$
{m}^{2}+4=0,
$$

which has roots $\pm 2i.$ Thus, the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\text{ and }{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡2x.
$$

Therefore, the matrix $A$ is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi ) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

and we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(0)(-1)-(-1)(0) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $det(A)=0$ we conclude that this BVP $\text{has infinitely many solutions.}$
